# Railway Overview

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- recognise the main elements of the railway
- identify the main parts of railway infrastructure
- explain the basic functions of track, points, signalling, overhead power, and telecommunications
- understand common railway terminology

## Introduction

At first glance a railway can look deceptively simple, however it is a system comprising many interconnected subsystems. All the various systems are vital to the safe and efficient running of a railway. It is of no use that the rails are intact if the signalling system is faulty, the overhead lines are not receiving power, or there is a fallen tree across the line. Although a signalling technician is primarily concerned with signalling equipment it can be necessary to work with other departments. This could include working with the track discipline (commonly known as “p-way”) when rails or switches need replaced, the Distribution and Plant discipline if there is a power failure, or the Off-Track discipline (who deal with fencing, vegetation, and access points) if vegetation is obscuring signals.

The railway can also often be accused of speaking its own language. To complicate things further, there are many colloquial and local terms, and in some cases the same thing may be referred to differently by different departments. It would be impossible to provide an exhaustive list of all such terms (indeed, *Ellis' British Railway Encyclopaedia* is nearly 600 pages and is not complete), but this should hopefully make some basic every day terms less mystifying. Signalling terminology can also differ from what you may be used to from other engineering backgrounds.

## The track

The most obvious part of railway infrastructure is the track. At first glance the track may appear to simply two rails, connected by sleepers, but in reality there is considerably more to it than that. A typical track construction includes:

- rails
- sleepers
- ballast
- the formation beneath the ballast
- rail fastenings to hold the rails to the sleepers
- switches and crossings to allow trains to change track
- expansion joints to accommodate for changes in temperature
- rail joints to connect lengths of track together, and insulated rail joints to provide electrical insulation

![Cross section of railway formation](https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcQzimfPAK6XTcSUShrHGTuXLRrKAa7VgFVYeTbT2hCQvpSaNCOdMyKUkjw&s=10)

### The rails

The rails provide the running surface and guide the train in the required direction. There are numerous types of rail, and although it's not necessary for a signalling technician to know the precise characteristics of each, there can be occasions where it is useful to know that there are variations. Historically rails with different shapes, or 'profiles', were used, but now almost all rail is of the flat-bottom type. There are three main types of flatbottom rail in use; BS113A, CEN60/UIC60, and CEN56. The numbers in the names relate to their weights, with BS113A weighing 113 lbs per yard, and CEN60 and CEN56 weighing 60 and 56 kg per meter respectively.

The rail profile, age, and manufacturer of the rail is brazed onto the side of the rail at regular intervals.

![Typical cross-section of flatbottom rail](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Dimitrios-Kostovasilis/publication/319542997/figure/fig1/AS:538010567823360@1505283123252/Typical-rail-cross-section-60E1.png){width="237"}

The rails are held securely to the sleepers by rail fastenings that fit into a metal baseplate attached to the sleeper. There are different types of rail fastenings, but the most commonly used are the Pandrol, or Pandrol fast-clip. Sometimes fastenings can also be used to secure signalling equipment.

### Sleepers

Sleepers are used to maintain the distance, or gauge, between the two rails. The UK uses something known as “Standard Gauge”, which is a distance of 4′8½″ (1,435 mm).

::: callout-caution
## Local trivia

The Glasgow Subway uses a slightly smaller track gauge of 4′ (1219 mm). It is the only passenger railway in Great Britain to not use Standard gauge outside of heritage lines.
:::

Sleepers can be made from reinforced concrete, wood, steel, or a polymer composite. Concrete sleepers are the most common, with other sleeper types more commonly used on slower speed lines or in depots.

::: callout-warning
### Warning

Wooden sleepers can be extremely slippery, especially in wet or frosty weather.
:::
